ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: New shortness of breath with wheeze and cough
- Symptom details: Onset 2–3 days ago after running; initially noted inability to converse while running; now dyspnea with brisk walking; wheeze and cough; no sputum; salbutamol (blue) inhaler provides little/no relief; using salbutamol daily and also prophylactically
- Severity/functional impact: Limits talking during run; dyspnea with brisk walking; requires frequent reliever use
- Aggravating/alleviating factors: Exertion worsens; salbutamol not helping; preventer (brown/Clenil) used twice daily
- Past medical history: Asthma; hay fever; possible eczema (patient suspects; family history positive). No prior asthma hospitalizations; last asthma attack 3–4 years ago; never used oral steroids
- Medications: Salbutamol (blue) PRN (currently daily and sometimes prophylactic); Clenil (beclomethasone, brown) preventer twice daily (previously 3 puffs BID per doctor, plan to increase to 4 puffs BID); topical cetraben and hydrocortisone for skin. No known drug allergies
- Family history: Brother with asthma; sister with eczema (atopy)
- Social history: Physically active (running). Smoking status not discussed. No recent travel/exposures mentioned
- Vitals/exam: None obtained (telehealth). No current peak flow performed; baseline/“when well” peak flow ~380 L/min per recall
- Labs/imaging: None

V: Pulmonary embolism: Acute exertional dyspnea could fit, but lacks risk factors, chest pain, tachycardia, hemoptysis; wheeze favors asthma
Spontaneous pneumothorax: Acute dyspnea can occur, but no pleuritic pain or unilateral findings reported
I: Viral upper respiratory infection/acute bronchitis: Can trigger asthma flare; patient has cough but no fever/sputum; onset over days
COVID-19: Could present with cough/dyspnea and trigger asthma, though no systemic symptoms reported
N: Endobronchial lesion: Could cause wheeze, but very unlikely given age and acute onset
D: Anemia: Can cause exertional dyspnea; does not explain wheeze; no supporting history
Deconditioning: Possible contributor but acute change over days and wheeze argue against
I2: Poor inhaler technique/nonadherence: Frequent SABA use with poor relief and confusion about meds suggests suboptimal controller use or technique
Medication-induced bronchospasm (e.g., NSAIDs/beta-blockers): Not reported but a potential trigger in asthmatics
C: Underlying atopic tendency: Family history of asthma/eczema supports atopy (predisposes to allergic asthma); not a distinct congenital disorder causing acute change
A: Allergic asthma flare: History of hay fever; seasonal/allergen exposure can precipitate wheeze and dyspnea
Allergic rhinitis with lower airway involvement: Upper airway allergy may exacerbate bronchospasm
T: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction: Symptoms first noticed during running; persists with brisk walking
Airway irritation from environmental exposure during exercise (e.g., cold air, pollutants): Could trigger bronchospasm
E: Thyrotoxicosis: Can cause dyspnea but unlikely with acute onset and wheeze
Pregnancy-related dyspnea: Not indicated in history

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Mild-to-moderate acute asthma exacerbation on background of persistent asthma
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic triad of wheeze, cough, and exertional dyspnea over 2–3 days in an atopic patient with known asthma; increased reliever use with inadequate relief suggests loss of control/exacerbation
supporting_evidence: Known asthma; last attack years ago but now with new symptoms
Dyspnea triggered by exertion and persisting afterward
Frequent salbutamol use with poor relief
Atopic history (hay fever; family with asthma/eczema)
opposing_evidence: No objective measures provided (no peak flow/SpO2) to grade severity
No clear infectious or allergen trigger explicitly identified

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB), contributing to current symptoms
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Symptoms first recognized during running and recur with brisk walking; EIB common in asthmatics and can present with chest tightness, wheeze, and dyspnea during/after exercise
supporting_evidence: Onset while running; worsens with brisk walking
Known asthma (EIB more common in asthmatics)
opposing_evidence: Symptoms now persist beyond exercise and over multiple days, suggesting broader asthma control issue rather than isolated EIB
Poor response to SABA may reflect technique/control rather than isolated EIB

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Allergic asthma flare driven by seasonal/environmental allergens
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Atopic history with hay fever and family atopy; allergen exposure commonly triggers asthma exacerbations, especially around seasonal changes
opposing_evidence: No explicit current nasal/ocular allergy symptoms reported
No identified allergen exposure in the transcript

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Viral upper respiratory infection/acute bronchitis triggering asthma
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Acute onset over days with cough could be viral, which is a frequent trigger of asthma exacerbations
opposing_evidence: No fever, myalgias, sore throat, or sputum production reported

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Poor inhaler technique or suboptimal controller regimen leading to loss of asthma control
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Frequent SABA use with poor relief and some confusion about medications suggest potential technique/adherence issues; last asthma review was 2 years ago
supporting_evidence: Using salbutamol daily and prophylactically with little benefit
Medication naming confusion (e.g., preventer specifics unclear)
Last structured asthma review 2 years ago
opposing_evidence: Patient reports using a preventer twice daily
Prior long period of control (last attack 3–4 years ago)
